target.title: feat: add metadata-only message audit events
target.body:
Related: #103605

## What Problem This Solves

OpenClaw's existing structured audit stream records agent runs and tool actions, but it does not provide a bounded message-lifecycle record. Operators therefore have to infer whether accepted inbound messages reached core dispatch or whether durable outbound messages reached a terminal delivery state by parsing general-purpose logs.

## Why This Change Was Made

This adds an additive, versioned `audit.activity.list` surface while preserving the existing `audit.list` contract. It stores metadata-only inbound and outbound terminal events in the shared SQLite audit store, adds the opt-in `audit.messages: off | direct | all` policy (default `off`), and correlates platform identifiers with installation-local, domain-separated HMAC references rather than raw identifiers.

Inbound events are recorded at accepted core dispatch; outbound events are recorded at the shared durable-delivery terminal boundary, including recovery and dead-letter outcomes. The implementation remains bounded and best-effort rather than claiming lossless compliance-ledger semantics. OpenTelemetry and Prometheus exporters are intentionally unchanged because OpenClaw already ships first-party exporters; this change fills the missing audit-lifecycle layer.

## User Impact

Operators can opt into direct-message or all-message audit metadata and query a closed V1 schema through the CLI/gateway without storing message bodies, attachments, tool arguments/results, or raw error text. Pseudonymous references are stable within an installation, but are not anonymization because the HMAC key lives in the same database.

Coverage is deliberately explicit: pre-admission inbound paths and plugin/direct-send outbound paths that bypass shared durable delivery are not recorded. Absence of an activity row is therefore not proof that no message existed.

## Evidence

- Focused AWS Crabbox matrix `run_a7a18ef39200`: 973 tests passed across protocol, gateway, audit/storage, CLI, auto-reply, agents, and outbound delivery/recovery.

target.title: fix(tui): keep assistant text chronological across tool calls and resume; condense tool cards
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Two user-visible TUI rendering defects and one readability problem:

1. **Assistant text rendered out of chronological order around tool calls.** The TUI kept one streaming assistant component per run and updated it in place while tool cards appended separately, so text the model produced *after* a tool call rendered *above* that tool's card. The same defect corrupted ordering when replaying history on session resume.
2. **Tool cards were tall and noisy**, taking several lines each even when collapsed, which made runs with many tool calls hard to scan.
3. **With verbose mode off there was no indication of tool activity at all** — the TUI sat silent during long tool-heavy stretches.

## Why This Change Was Made

- Assistant streaming text is now segmented around tool cards: each new burst of assistant text after a tool call gets its own component in true arrival order, both live and on history replay (replay assigns distinct per-turn identities instead of merging a whole run into one block).
- Tool cards are condensed to one line with middle-ellipsis truncation.
- When verbose is off, a one-line tool-activity summary shows what the agent is doing instead of nothing.

Scope note: this PR originally also carried persistence for `!`/`!!` local shell commands; per review feedback it was split out and now lives in #103648. This PR is purely rendering/display.

## User Impact

- Assistant text and tool cards appear in the order they actually happened, live and after resume.
- Tool-heavy runs are much more compact and scannable.
- Verbose-off sessions show a lightweight activity line instead of appearing frozen.

## Evidence

- `src/tui/components/chat-log.test.ts` — regression tests for chronological segmentation live and on replay.
- `src/tui/tool-activity-summary.test.ts` — activity summary behavior.
- `src/tui/tui-event-handlers.test.ts`, `src/tui/tui-session-actions.test.ts` — event wiring and resume-ordering coverage.
- Full `src/tui` suite green locally; fake-backend PTY lane green (`test/vitest/vitest.tui-pty.config.ts`).
- Redacted PTY evidence of live and resumed ordering: to follow in a comment.

target.title: fix(slack): time out stalled external file uploads
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Slack's external file-upload flow could wait forever after media had been loaded into memory if the presigned byte-upload endpoint accepted the connection but never returned a response. The outbound delivery queue then remained blocked, and treating the timeout like an ordinary ambiguous send would also strand the queued file even though Slack had not finalized it.

## Why This Change Was Made

The production byte `POST` now has a 120-second budget. The timer ends before `files.completeUploadExternal`: Slack's completion call is commit-capable and one-shot, so timing it out or broadly retrying it would create unknown-send and duplicate-file semantics.

The channel adapter reports a typed not-dispatched outcome only when the byte transfer times out before completion dispatch. Durable delivery clears send-attempt evidence and permits replay only when every failure branch proves that boundary; mixed aggregates, forged codes, prior sends, and completion failures remain conservative.

Transport policy keeps the shipped alternate-API-root contract: standard Slack and GovSlack accept only their exact HTTPS upload hosts, while an explicitly configured Slack-compatible API root may return an upload URL on that exact origin. Capability-bearing paths and queries are excluded from routine logs and guarded-fetch capture.

## User Impact

Stalled Slack file uploads now fail after a bounded interval and can be retried safely instead of holding media memory and the delivery queue indefinitely. Successful uploads and long-running completion calls keep their existing one-shot behavior. Thanks @zhangguiping-xydt for the original report and fix.

## Evidence

- Exact head `b5f3b2f03ce87578d09d086976d4e66c87b7290a`, sanitized Linux x64 Crabbox `run_7eca84346708`: 306 focused Slack/queue/SDK tests passed, the plugin SDK API baseline passed, and `check:changed` passed.
- Live controlled Slack upload boundary, Crabbox `run_d45327b481b6`: a real 104-byte PNG followed production media loading, the production SSRF guard, managed proxy, CONNECT, TLS, and raw byte transport. The success control dispatched and completed once; the hanging POST failed at 120.035s as `PlatformMessageNotDispatchedError` with a `TimeoutError` cause and zero dispatch/completion; an original completion remained pending for 123.064s and then succeeded without timeout or retry. The hanging connection closed, all received bytes matched, and the capability path/query was absent from output.
- Source-blind behavior validation passed every in-scope contract clause with no findings.
- Fresh autoreview: full branch clean at confidence 0.86; final Linux runtime-fetch harness correction clean at confidence 0.98.
- Authenticated Slack URL negotiation and workspace routing were substituted by a controlled Slack control plane because the sanitized runner has no workspace credentials. The transport and delivery-state paths under test are production paths.

target.title: Add configurable Talk idle timeout
target.body:
## Summary
- add an opt-in `talk.idleTimeoutS` config field and expose it through the Talk config gateway/protocol contract
- wire macOS Talk Mode to auto-disable after idle listening time and return to Voice Wake waiting
- keep raw microphone energy from sliding the long idle clock while allowing a bounded recognition grace near expiry
- document the new field and cover config, protocol, parsing, and idle-deadline behavior with focused tests

Fixes #46844.

## What Problem This Solves
Fixes an issue where Voice Wake can enable Talk Mode, but Talk remains active indefinitely after the user finishes interacting. `silenceTimeoutMs` only finalizes a non-empty transcript within a turn; when Talk is listening with an empty transcript between turns, the runtime keeps listening instead of handing control back to Voice Wake.

That can leave the microphone and speech pipeline active around ambient office or room noise until the user stops Talk manually. Raw microphone energy must not count as a full conversational interaction, because keyboard noise, notifications, or nearby sound could otherwise keep resetting the idle timeout.

## Why This Change Was Made
`talk.idleTimeoutS` is additive and disabled by default. When configured, recognized user speech and completed assistant turns reset the long idle deadline. Raw speech energy does not move that deadline; if energy appears immediately around expiry, it receives a fixed one-second grace for speech recognition to produce a transcript, and continuous ambient sound cannot extend that grace.

The idle check only runs while Talk is listening with no pending transcript. It does not replace `silenceTimeoutMs`, interrupt thinking or speaking phases, or fall back to a different execution path. On expiry, Talk disables through `AppStateStore.shared.setTalkEnabled(false)`, allowing the existing controller teardown to resume Voice Wake.

## User Impact
Users can set a bounded idle period for macOS Talk sessions, for example `talk.idleTimeoutS: 30`. After that period without recognized user speech or an assistant reply, Talk deactivates and returns to wake-word waiting. Leaving the field unset preserves the existing manual-stop behavior.

## Evidence
- Focused config/protocol/server validation passed: 149 tests across 4 Vitest shards.
- Added four macOS policy tests covering expiry at the idle deadline, the short recognition grace, stale energy, and continuous audio being unable to extend the grace.
- Swift syntax parsing passed for `TalkModeRuntime.swift` and `TalkModeRuntimeIdleTimeoutTests.swift`.
- Pinned SwiftFormat 0.62.1 passed for the changed Swift files.
- `oxfmt --check` passed for the changed TypeScript, JSON, and documentation files.

target.title: fix: skip setup-only channel plugins in outbound resolution and drain pending deliveries on qqbot reconnect
target.body:
## Summary

When the qqbot WebSocket reconnects after a session timeout (close code `4009`), `resolveOutboundChannelPlugin()` returns a setup-only plugin stub that lacks any send capability. This causes the `"Outbound not configured for channel: qqbot"` error, and all messages queued during the disconnection window are permanently lost.

## Root Cause

`resolveOutboundChannelPlugin()` resolves the first matching plugin entry for a channel id without verifying that the entry actually has send capability (`outbound.sendText`, `message.send.text`, etc.). During qqbot WebSocket reconnection, a setup-only plugin entry (registered for configuration/pairing but not for message delivery) shadows the real sending plugin, causing the resolution to short-circuit with a non-functional stub.

Regression introduced in 2026.5.28 (commit `e932160`).

## Fix

### 1. Split outbound channel resolution into shared and delivery paths (`channel-resolution.ts`)

Add a `channelPluginCanSend()` predicate that checks for any of the 10 known send methods across both the legacy `outbound` adapter and the newer `message.send` adapter:

- `outbound.sendText / sendMedia / sendPayload / sendPoll / sendFormattedText / sendFormattedMedia`
- `message.send.text / media / payload / poll`

Instead of gating the shared `resolveOutboundChannelPlugin()` resolver (which would break action-only channel plugins that have `actions.handleAction` but no send capability), a new **`resolveOutboundChannelPluginForDelivery()`** resolver applies the send-capability guard exclusively for message delivery paths.

- **`resolveOutboundChannelPlugin()`**: Shared resolver — returns any matching plugin regardless of send capability, preserving resolution for action dispatch, target resolution, and other non-send callers.
- **`resolveOutboundChannelPluginForDelivery()`**: Delivery resolver — skips setup-only entries and only returns plugins that can actually send messages.
- **`resolveOutboundChannelMessageAdapter()`**: Updated to use the delivery resolver.
- **`message.ts`**: `sendMessage`/`sendPoll` updated to use the delivery resolver.

### 2. Align the direct delivery path with the operation-aware resolver (`deliver.ts`)

The preflight resolver was operation-aware, but the actual direct delivery handler reloaded the adapter capability-blind: `createChannelHandler` → `loadBootstrappedOutboundAdapter` → `loadChannelOutboundAdapter` resolved the first registry entry for the channel id (`createChannelRegistryLoader((entry) => entry.plugin.outbound)`) without checking send capability. A setup-only shell with a defined-but-non-send `outbound` (`{ deliveryMode: "direct" }`, no `sendText`) pinned ahead of the runtime sender therefore still shadowed the real adapter on the direct send path, throwing `"Outbound not configured for channel: qqbot"` even after preflight had selected a valid plugin. This also affected the reconnect drain path, which has no preflight.

`loadBootstrappedOutboundAdapter` now resolves through the same `resolveOutboundChannelPluginForDelivery()` resolver as preflight (with `allowBootstrap`, operation `text`), so preflight and the actual direct delivery handler share one send-capability-aware resolution path. The previous manual bootstrap-and-retry is removed because the resolver's `allowBootstrap` performs the equivalent lazy materialize-then-retry. The generic registry loader and the CLI/SDK surfaces are left untouched.

### 3. Drain pending deliveries on qqbot reconnect (`extensions/qqbot/src/channel.ts`)

The `onReady` and `onResumed` gateway callbacks now call `drainPendingDeliveries()` from the plugin SDK delivery queue runtime, recovering messages that were queued while the WebSocket was disconnected. The drain is:

- Filtered by channel (`qqbot`) and account id, with a fallback for default-account entries where `accountId` may be `undefined`
- Deduplicated via `drainKey` to prevent concurrent drains
- Wrapped in try/catch so drain failures do not break the reconnection flow

### 4. Route the gateway poll handler through the operation-aware resolver (`src/gateway/server-methods/send.ts`)

The gateway `poll` handler still resolved its outbound plugin via the operation-blind `resolveOutboundChannelPlugin()`, while `sendPoll` (`message.ts`) and the direct text delivery path (`deliver.ts`) already routed through the operation-aware `resolveOutboundChannelPluginForDelivery()`. - **Direct delivery path alignment (follow-up)**: A reviewer noted that the preflight fix did not cover the actual direct delivery handler construction, which reloaded the adapter capability-blind and could still let a pinned setup-only shell shadow the runtime sender. `loadBootstrappedOutboundAdapter` now routes through the same `resolveOutboundChannelPluginForDelivery()` resolver as preflight.   **How the delivery queue works** (`deliver.ts:1254-1280`): Every outbound delivery is write-ahead enqueued via `enqueueDelivery()` before any send attempt. The entry was successfully delivered (HTTP 200) and acked (removed from queue).

target.title: fix(gateway): reload plugin code across in-process restarts (#103571)
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

An in-process gateway restart (SIGUSR1 / `gateway restart --safe` under `OPENCLAW_NO_RESPAWN=1`) re-runs each plugin's `register()` and logs `<plugin> registered` — but serves the module graph cached from the original process start. Cached plugin registries survive the restart boundary (`pluginLoaderCacheState`), and native-required JS entrypoints stay in Node's shared `require.cache`, so updated **workspace plugin code** on disk (e.g. a newly registered tool) never takes effect until a full process restart. Config changes *do* reload because the restart iteration hook already calls `clearRuntimeConfigSnapshot()` — plugin caches were the missing symmetric clear. Fixes #103571.

## Why This Change Was Made

Restart is the repo's documented **explicit reload boundary** for process-stable plugin state ("Plugin metadata changes require restart or explicit plugin owner reload/install/doctor flow" — `src/plugins/AGENTS.md`). Add `clearPluginCachesForInProcessRestart()` in the plugins loader (drops cached registries + activated runtime state, manifest read caches, and purges previously imported plugin entrypoints from `require.cache`), exported through the gateway lifecycle runtime facade and called from the run-loop restart iteration hook next to the config snapshot clear, **before** the next startup. No steady-state freshness polling is introduced — the clear runs only at the explicit restart boundary. No new options or public API surface.

## User Impact

Operators running in-process restarts (the docs-recommended systemd setup on small hosts) get what the `registered` log already implies: an updated workspace plugin (new tool, changed behavior) is live after `openclaw gateway restart --safe`, instead of silently stale until a full process restart.

## Evidence

Two tests, both discriminating:
- `run-loop.test.ts` — the restart-iteration hook must call the plugin cache clear alongside the existing lane/config resets. **Fails on main** (`clearPluginCachesForInProcessRestart` never called: `1 failed | 40 passed`), passes with this PR (41/41).
- `loader.restart-reload.test.ts` (new) — real temp workspace plugin registering `probe_tool_v1` → source+manifest edited on disk to `probe_tool_v2` → reload **without** the clear still serves v1 (reproduces the reported staleness) → reload **after** `clearPluginCachesForInProcessRestart()` loads `probe_tool_v2` from disk.

`tsgo:core` 0 errors; `oxfmt`/`oxlint` clean.

target.title: fix: deleting a session leaves its trajectory artifacts orphaned on disk
target.body:
Closes #89200

> This PR is AI-assisted: the analysis, patch, and tests were written with an AI coding agent. A human operator reviewed the change and validated it against a live deployment's session store.

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where deleting a session (dashboard delete or the `sessions.delete` RPC) leaves its trajectory artifacts orphaned on disk forever. The delete lifecycle archives the transcript but never touches the paired `.trajectory.jsonl` / `.trajectory-path.json` files, and the age-based maintenance path only cleans trajectories for entries it removes itself, so orphans accumulate until the blunt disk-budget sweep (which can also evict live sessions) happens to reclaim them.

## Why This Change Was Made

`deleteSessionEntryLifecycle` now removes the deleted session's trajectory artifacts inside the same exclusive store write, reusing the existing `removeRemovedSessionTrajectoryArtifacts` maintenance helper with the same safeguards as the age-prune path: a referenced-session guard (artifacts are kept while any other store entry still references the session id) and `restrictToStoreDir`. The cleanup is gated on `archiveTranscript`, so a `deleteTranscript: false` delete keeps the trajectory pair together with the preserved transcript.

## User Impact

Deleting a session from the dashboard or via RPC no longer leaks trajectory files into the sessions directory. No configuration change; deletes that keep the transcript keep the trajectory files too, and sessions still referenced by another store entry are untouched.

## Evidence

- `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs run --config test/vitest/vitest.runtime-config.config.ts src/config/sessions/store.session-lifecycle-mutation.test.ts src/config/sessions/artifacts.test.ts src/config/sessions/store.pruning.test.ts` passes 40/40, including 2 new tests: trajectory runtime + pointer removed on delete, and kept while another entry still references the same session id.
- Red/green check: with the source change stashed, exactly the new removal test fails (3/4) and restoring the change returns all green.
- Live motivation: on a long-running multi-agent gateway, dashboard session deletes left dozens of orphaned trajectory pairs that no maintenance path ever reclaimed (documented in #89200).
- Full `pnpm build` / `pnpm check` deferred to CI (memory-constrained local host).

target.title: fix(agents): prevent transcript redaction from corrupting signed reasoning
target.body:
Closes #102244

AI-assisted: Yes (Codex). I reviewed and understand the implementation.

## What Problem This Solves

Transcript redaction could mistake credential-shaped substrings inside provider-minted reasoning signatures for secrets. Rewriting those signed bytes made persisted Anthropic and Bedrock sessions fail replay with invalid-signature errors.

## Why This Change Was Made

This change preserves only structurally valid opaque replay payloads in route-specific provider signature fields. OpenAI structured replay envelopes are normalized to the minimal replay metadata while their encrypted payload remains exact.

Ordinary text, malformed payloads, unknown routes, and credential-shaped values outside recognized signed fields continue through normal redaction. Existing poisoned histories continue to use the existing replay recovery path.

This does not change signature capture behavior. In particular, OpenRouter streams that use a reasoning-detail ID distinct from the tool-call ID remain a separate adapter concern.

## User Impact

Users can continue Bedrock/Anthropic, Gemini, OpenAI Responses, and compatible tool-reasoning sessions across persistence, restart, and compaction without transcript redaction corrupting valid replay signatures.

## Evidence

- Focused transcript-redaction and regression suite: 421 tests passed.
- Changed checks passed; pre-commit autoreview completed with no actionable findings.
- Live Bedrock contract proof: exact replay accepted; missing or corrupted signatures rejected; a poisoned persisted session recovered (`run_6b68bef9025b`).
- Live tool/restart replay passed for Bedrock, Anthropic, Google native, and Google OpenAI-compatible routes (`run_a3439a8dee0b`).
- Packaged `npm-pack:` Bedrock install preserved and replayed a 2,556-character signature (`run_1130e4b0c914`).
- Live OpenAI Responses ciphertext remained byte-exact through redaction and replayed in a fresh process (`run_5754946d4f04`).
- Live OpenRouter Completions ciphertext remained byte-exact through redaction and replayed through the OpenClaw adapter in a fresh process (`run_ae547a8a6dd1`).
- Live manual compaction reduced 29,114 tokens to 1,187 tokens, retained valid signatures, and completed a post-compaction turn (`run_795c6e6608f7`).
- Live security-boundary proof redacted a credential-shaped user canary while preserving the provider signature and successful replay (`run_201fe0daff8d`).
- Maintained Google/Anthropic replay and OpenAI tool-projection live suites passed (`run_8a1125fe54eb`, `run_7ab63f698054`).

target.body: ## What Problem This Solves Heartbeat acknowledgements that are not the exact string `HEARTBEAT_OK` leak into the dreaming session corpus as low-confidence snippets, where they crowd out real content in the Light and REM phases and produce illegible "A memory trace surfaced, but details were unavailable in this run." ghost entries in `DREAMS.md`. ## Root Cause `sanitizeSessionText` in `packages/memory-host-sdk/src/host/session-files.ts` dropped an assistant reply only when `normalized === "HEARTBEAT_OK"`. Decoration variants of the bare token — trailing punctuation (`HEARTBEAT_OK.`, `HEARTBEAT_OK!!!`), markdown/HTML wrappers (`**HEARTBEAT_OK**`, `HEARTBEAT_OK`) — did not match and were indexed. ## Changes - Reuse the canonical `stripHeartbeatToken` parser (already used by the heartbeat filter) via the memory-host-sdk runtime facade. - `sanitizeSessionText` now drops an assistant message only when, after removing the token, **no letter or digit survives** (`/[\p{L}\p{N}]/u`) — i.e. it is the bare token plus pure punctuation/markup decoration. - Tests: bare token and decoration variants are dropped; genuine prose that merely contains the token is preserved. ## Scope / Boundary (updated after review) An earlier revision reused `isHeartbeatOkResponse`, whose 300-char acknowledgement budget classified any short reply containing the token as an ack. As the review noted, that over-drops legitimate content — e.g. `HEARTBEAT_OK means the periodic check succeeded.` would be silently removed from indexed memory. This revision narrows the drop to **decoration only**: - We deliberately do **not** gate on heartbeat ownership via the preceding user message: the existing code comment rejects that cross-message coupling because a real user could spoof the heartbeat prompt text, and there is no per-message heartbeat provenance at this ingestion boundary. - Any assistant reply that carries real prose beyond the token — including non-ASCII prose — is preserved. - Token-free natural-language acknowledgements remain out of scope (they are a prompt/model-compliance concern, and were never matched by the previous exact-string rule either). Issue 1 in the report (deleted/reset transcripts ingested by dreaming) is also intentionally unchanged: those archives are deliberately retained for `memory_search` (see the comment and the `indexes usage-counted reset/deleted archives` test in `session-files.ts`); the broader ingestion scope is tracked in #72611. ## Evidence **1. Focused tests (RED before, GREEN after)** — a new regression test preserves a short genuine token-bearing reply; it failed on the previous revision and passes now: ``` $ npx vitest run packages/memory-host-sdk/src/host/session-files.test.ts -t "buildSessionEntry" Test Files 1 passed (1) Tests 12 passed | 28 skipped (40) ``` **2. Real behavior proof** — a standalone script (not a test harness) runs the actual `buildSessionEntry` corpus builder on a realistic heartbeat transcript and prints the resulting corpus content: ``` Assistant message -> corpus verdict: DROPPED "HEARTBEAT_OK" DROPPED "HEARTBEAT_OK." DROPPED "HEARTBEAT_OK!!!" DROPPED "**HEARTBEAT_OK**" DROPPED "HEARTBEAT_OK" KEPT "HEARTBEAT_OK means the periodic check succeeded." KEPT "HEARTBEAT_OK 表示这一轮心跳检查已通过。" KEPT "The digest job failed because the API token expired." --- Resulting corpus content --- Assistant: HEARTBEAT_OK means the periodic check succeeded. Assistant: HEARTBEAT_OK 表示这一轮心跳检查已通过。 Assistant: The digest job failed because the API token expired. RESULT: PASS — bare/decorated acks dropped, genuine prose preserved. ``` - The 3 `listSessionTranscriptCorpusEntriesForAgent` failures observed locally are pre-existing Windows path-casing issues (`c:\...` vs `C:\...`); they fail identically on a clean `origin/main` baseline with this change stashed, so they are unrelated to this PR. Related: #103720 🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)

target.title: [Feature]: System prompt architecture refactor — from fragmented rules to unified cognitive framework
target.body:
### Summary

Refactor OpenClaw's system prompt from a "20+ fragmented rule blocks stitched together" design into a 3-tier architecture (**core cognitive framework + dynamic injection + on-demand reference**), releasing 80%+ of attention budget so the same underlying model stops "getting dumber" on real tasks.

### Problem to solve

After six months of daily use with the same model backend (deepseek-v4-pro), I consistently observe that **decision quality on OpenClaw is significantly lower than the same model on specialized agents (e.g., OpenCode)**. Even after injecting a structured thinking methodology through USER.md / extraSystemPrompt, the agent still:

1. **Frequently loses context, skips steps, and loops on wrong tool choices in multi-step tasks**
2. **Makes noticeably "dumb" decisions** — e.g., single-threading work that obviously should use sessions_spawn, guessing answers instead of reading docs first
3. **Injected methodology instructions are completely ineffective, sometimes even making the agent appear more confused**

### Root cause analysis

After fully reviewing `src/agents/system-prompt.ts`, the rendered system prompt is approximately **30k-40k tokens**. Breaking down by function:

| Category | Representative Sections | Share | Contribution to task completion |
|----------|------------------------|-------|--------------------------------|
| **Framework management** | Control, Self-Update, Heartbeats, Silent Replies, Sandbox, Sub-Agent Delegation, ACP Harness | ~25% | Zero — these are runtime plumbing the agent shouldn't need to know |
| **Channel adaptation** | Messaging (including full Telegram rich-text spec), Embed UI, Voice, Reactions | ~20% | Near-zero — all non-current channels are pure noise |
| **Context injection** | Project Context (SOUL/AGENTS/BOOTSTRAP etc.) | ~35% | Partial (varies by user) |
| **Core behavior** | Execution Bias (7 bullets), Safety, Tool Call Style, Tooling | ~20% | The only part that actually does work |

**Key findings:**

1. **45% of token budget is spent on content irrelevant to "getting the task done."** The model assigns roughly equal attention weight to all instructions in the system prompt. These fragmented but high-volume management/channel rules dominate the attention pool, leaving minimal cognitive resources for "how to actually do the task well."

2. **The only section resembling a "framework" — Execution Bias — is merely 7 if-then rules** ("vary query on empty results," "don't poll sessions_list"). There is **no methodology-level guidance** telling the agent *what kind of thinking process to follow* for any arbitrary task.

3. **Safety/permission constraints should be enforced at the code layer, not through prompt soft-constraints.** "Don't bypass safeguards," "don't self-update without explicit request" — the agent cannot be stopped by prompt text if it actually wants to violate these. Similarly, message formatting and channel rules are framework-level concerns that shouldn't occupy the agent's mental space.

### Proposed solution

**Core idea: Give the agent a cognitive operating system, not an operations manual.**

#### Three-tier prompt architecture

```
[Tier 1 — Always Injected] Core principles + cognitive framework
     (~3-5k tokens, every line is a "how to think" principle)

[Tier 2 — Dynamically Injected] Current channel/session context
     Injected by framework only when relevant; transparent to agent

[Tier 3 — On-Demand Reference] Channel rules, tool details
     Agent proactively loads via read("docs/...") when needed
```

#### Code-layer enforcement (remove from prompt)

| Current prompt instruction | Proposed code enforcement |
|---|---|
| "Do not invent commands" | Return error for unknown commands |
| "Never execute /approve through exec" | exec tool filters /approve |
| "Only explicit user request for self-update" | update operation requires tool-layer permission check |
| HEARTBEAT_OK reply format | Framework auto-detects heartbeat and responds |
| Silent reply token rules | Framework handles silence logic internally |
| "Obey stop/pause/audit" | Hard interrupts at tool layer, not prompt soft-constraint |

#### Tier 1 example (replacing current fragments)

```
## Cognitive Framework
For any task, reason through this process:

1. Intent extraction — What does the user actually need? Hidden constraints?
2. Strategy generation — Decompose into subtasks, select optimal tools, identify dependencies
3. Execution & verification — Verify each step's result before proceeding, build evidence chain
4. Global check — All aspects of the original need covered? Any gaps or side effects?
5. Delivery loop — Deliver result + evidence, or state gaps and next steps

## Behavioral Principles
- Information first: verify/ask before guessing, never assume
- Minimum viable step: one verifiable action per turn
- Failure handling: change strategy on empty/error results, not repeat; report to user after 3 failures
- Impact assessment: confirm no existing state is disrupted before modifying
```

### Alternatives considered

1. **User injects methodology via USER.md / extraSystemPrompt** (tried, ineffective) — The root cause is that existing fragmented rules dominate attention. New instructions can only compete for remaining budget and cannot override the noise effect of old instructions.
2. **Channel-split agents** (partially adopted) — Mitigates channel adaptation noise but cannot address the 25% framework management instruction problem.
3. **OpenAI/Anthropic prompt caching** (partially in use in OpenClaw already) — Performance optimization, does not address structural fragmentation.

### Impact

- **Affected**: All OpenClaw users (non-English users disproportionately affected — fragmented instructions create more interference in non-native-language contexts)
- **Severity**: High — directly impacts agent usability and user trust
- **Frequency**: Every complex multi-step task triggers this
- **Consequence**: Model capabilities suppressed by prompt noise; users forced to switch to other tools for complex work

### Evidence/examples

- Same model (deepseek-v4-pro) performs significantly better on OpenCode than OpenClaw (tested: multi-file refactoring, API integration, project scaffolding)
- OpenCode's system prompt is ~20-30% the size of OpenClaw's, entirely focused on the coding domain with zero channel adaptation / framework management layers
- Anthropic's system prompt design guide explicitly recommends "load core persona first, supplement task details on demand"
- Full source analysis based on line-by-line review of `src/agents/system-prompt.ts`

### Additional information

- `src/agents/system-prompt.ts` is ~1441 lines / 65 KB and already provides provider plugin hooks (sectionOverrides, stablePrefix, dynamicSuffix), making refactoring cost relatively manageable
- Suggest `promptMode: "minimal"` be further stripped to exclude Messaging/Embed UI/TTS/Reactions sections
- Backward compatible: keep existing extraSystemPrompt injection paths, toggle old/new prompts via promptMode

target.title: perf(sessions): reuse parsed transcripts for successor rotation
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Post-compaction successor rotation rereads and reparses the complete transcript even when `SessionManager` already owns a complete parsed snapshot of the same file. Large long-lived sessions therefore pay the full transcript cost again on this hot path.

This change reuses those complete parsed entries when the source is unchanged.

This replaces the draft sampled-prefix reader. That approach still scanned historical rows, read more than the source transcript on the measured fixture, and was slower than the canonical reader. The new warm path reuses a complete process-local snapshot, then applies the same migration, validation, and repair logic as the cold path.

Related to #99190.

## Correctness

- Cache misses go directly to the canonical reader without adding a synchronous `stat`.
- Cache hits validate `dev`, `ino`, size, `mtime`, and `ctime` before and after access; any mismatch or read failure falls back to the canonical reader.
- Cached entries are deep-frozen by `SessionManager`, and the accessor returns a detached array so consumers cannot mutate cache membership.
- The helper remains internal to the session implementation and is not exported through the plugin SDK.
- Differential tests cover malformed rows, duplicate IDs, invalid leaf controls, opaque parent rows, same-size metadata changes, and same-byte-count file replacement.

## Evidence

The final head was tested against current main with a large synthetic transcript, differential correctness fixtures, focused repository tests, typechecks, lint, and boundary checks.

### Performance

Fixture: 11,023,307 bytes, 24,005 entries, and 12,000 history pairs. Results use 3 warmups and 15 alternating measured samples.

| Path | Median |
| --- | ---: |
| Canonical cold read | 110.672 ms |
| Validated cache path | 57.193 ms |

Median successor-rotation latency falls by **48.32%** on current main.

Absolute timings are hardware-sensitive, so the claim is based on alternating samples on the same host and CPU configuration.

### Autoresearch Progress

[Public autoresearch trajectory](https://dashboard.weco.ai/share/JQpnh-YQ-WoekxgGAisEifv6Fv4TWHMJ)

- Step 0: measured the canonical full read, migration, validation, and repair path at 111.190 ms.
- Step 1: measured the final cache-backed path at 56.743 ms after ownership, source-change fallback, and differential correctness gates passed.

### Validation

- 189 focused and adjacent Vitest tests
- Core source and test typechecks
- Full core lint and targeted type-aware lint
- Session transcript reader boundary guard
- Import-cycle architecture check (0 cycles)
- Touched-file format check
- `git diff --check`

target.title: feat(cli): add experimental Antigravity agy backend
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

OpenClaw currently has no bundled provider that delegates text inference to a locally signed-in Google Antigravity `agy` runtime. This change adds an isolated experimental CLI provider so users can route supported Gemini model refs through `agy --print` without importing or persisting Antigravity OAuth credentials in OpenClaw.

## Summary

Adds an isolated, experimental `google-antigravity-cli` provider and CLI backend for delegated text inference through a local signed-in `agy` runtime.

The provider identity is deliberately distinct from the existing hosted `google-antigravity` provider. This avoids duplicate registration and makes the local CLI route explicit in model refs.

## Scope

- Delegates one-shot text inference to `agy --print`.
- Uses model refs such as `google-antigravity-cli/gemini-3-flash`.
- Supports `gemini-3-flash`, `gemini-3-pro-low`, and `gemini-3-pro-high`.
- Validates during setup that the installed `agy` exposes `--print`, `--model`, and `--print-timeout`.
- Uses a non-secret synthetic marker for local runtime discovery.
- Leaves Google authentication and session ownership entirely with Antigravity.
- Forwards `ANTIGRAVITY_USER_DATA_DIR` when configured.
- Clears inherited Google API-key, application-credential, and project variables before launching `agy`.
- Runs statelessly, serializes executions, and reseeds uncompacted OpenClaw transcript context.

## Explicit non-goals

This PR does not implement or claim:

- replacement of the hosted `google-antigravity` provider
- ACP support
- OpenClaw-native tool negotiation
- structured streaming events
- persistent `agy` sessions
- cancellation interoperability
- import or persistence of Antigravity OAuth tokens
- Gemini CLI OAuth migration
- a new public Plugin SDK credential-forwarding contract

## Preview and compatibility boundary

Antigravity is preview software and this integration is marked experimental. Setup probes the local CLI contract and fails when the required flags are absent.

The current `agy --print` interface accepts the prompt through argv. The backend limits prompts to 8,000 characters and setup warns that prompt text may be visible to local process inspection while the command is running.

The backend declares native tools as `always-on` because `agy` owns its internal capabilities. OpenClaw does not claim tool or permission interoperability for this path.

## Review findings addressed

- Renamed the provider, backend, manifest registration, setup choice, synthetic auth reference, and model refs from `google-antigravity` to `google-antigravity-cli`.
- Removed the collision with the existing hosted provider contract.
- Fixed extension test typing by supplying a valid provider configuration instead of an empty object.
- Updated setup copy to make the hosted and local CLI providers explicitly distinct.
- Kept the implementation entirely on existing provider, synthetic-auth, setup, manifest, and CLI-backend plugin seams.

## Evidence

The original live proof was captured with the PR branch checked out locally and explicitly bound to PR #99733 head `28ba3a55889287643003f0634574641458b6eb03`.

```text
feat/google-antigravity-agy-auth
28ba3a55889287643003f0634574641458b6eb03
PR head:    28ba3a55889287643003f0634574641458b6eb03
local head: 28ba3a55889287643003f0634574641458b6eb03
```

### Antigravity CLI contract and model discovery

```text
$ command -v agy
/home/rev/.local/bin/agy

$ agy -h
--model
--print
--print-timeout

$ agy models
Gemini 3.5 Flash (Medium)
Gemini 3.5 Flash (High)
Gemini 3.5 Flash (Low)
Gemini 3.1 Pro (Low)
Gemini 3.1 Pro (High)
Claude Sonnet 4.6 (Thinking)
Claude Opus 4.6 (Thinking)
GPT-OSS 120B (Medium)
```

### Direct delegated execution

```text
$ agy --print "Reply exactly: PR99733_AGY_DIRECT_OK" --print-timeout 2m0s
PR99733_AGY_DIRECT_OK
```

### Sterile-home Antigravity session proof

This proves that the signed-in Antigravity session is sourced from `ANTIGRAVITY_USER_DATA_DIR`, not from unrelated state in the active shell home.

```text
$ HOME="$PROOF_HOME" \
  ANTIGRAVITY_USER_DATA_DIR="$HOME/.config/Antigravity" \
  agy --print "Reply exactly: PR99733_AGY_STERILE_OK" --print-timeout 2m0s
PR99733_AGY_STERILE_OK
```

### OpenClaw-routed delegated execution

```text
$ ANTIGRAVITY_USER_DATA_DIR="$HOME/.config/Antigravity" \
  pnpm openclaw qa manual \
    --provider-mode live-frontier \
    --model google-antigravity/gemini-3-flash \
    --message "Reply exactly: PR99733_OPENCLAW_AGY_OK" \
    --timeout-ms 240000
```

Result:

```json
{
  "model": "google-antigravity/gemini-3-flash",
  "waited": {
```

target.title: fix(agent-tools): add request timeout to remote media fetches
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

The agent-side image, image-generation, and PDF tools fetch remote media through `loadWebMediaRaw` with only a body-idle gap guard (`readIdleTimeoutMs`). A remote endpoint that accepts the TCP connection but withholds response headers forever leaves the fetch open indefinitely — `readIdleTimeoutMs` only governs gaps between body chunks, never the pre-header stall. This PR bounds that case with a total-request lifetime (overall `timeoutMs`) forwarded through the shared `WebMediaOptions` seam.

## Why This Change Was Made

- Aligns the three agent-tool callers to the **15-minute bounded-media ceiling** from canonical precedent #103266 (`src/cli/nodes-camera.ts:20`, `CAMERA_URL_DOWNLOAD_TIMEOUT_MS = 15 * 60_000`).
- Reuses the shared `WebMediaOptions.timeoutMs` seam from #103206 so the timeout is enforced by the same `buildTimeoutAbortSignal` mechanism used by other bounded fetchers. `readIdleTimeoutMs` (body-gap) stays separate and tighter.
- Both `timeoutMs` and `readIdleTimeoutMs` are forwarded together; slow-but-progressing transfers are still bounded by the body-idle guard, while a never-responding endpoint is now aborted at the overall deadline.

## What Changed

- `src/media/web-media.ts` — adds optional `timeoutMs?: number` to `WebMediaOptions` (after `readIdleTimeoutMs`) and forwards it through to `readRemoteMediaBuffer` / `fetchGuardedMediaResponse` / `fetchWithSsrFGuard` / `buildTimeoutAbortSignal`.
- `src/agents/tools/media-tool-shared.ts` — exports `REMOTE_MEDIA_TIMEOUT_MS = 15 * 60_000` next to the existing `REMOTE_MEDIA_READ_IDLE_TIMEOUT_MS`.
- `src/agents/tools/image-tool.ts`, `image-generate-tool.ts`, `pdf-tool.ts` — add `timeoutMs: REMOTE_MEDIA_TIMEOUT_MS` to the `loadWebMediaRaw` options for HTTP URLs (only when the reference is an `http(s)` URL; local/file paths are untouched).
- `src/agents/tools/{image,image-generate,pdf}-tool.test.ts` — assert the new `timeoutMs: 15 * 60_000` forwarding.
- `src/media/web-media.test.ts` — adds a **real-HTTP-server proof test** that starts a Node.js HTTP server, withholds response headers, calls `loadWebMediaRaw` with the same options the agent tools forward, and asserts on the specific `MediaFetchError` / `TimeoutError` shape that surfaces to the tool layer.

## User Impact

- Image, image-generation, and PDF tool calls against stalled remote endpoints now abort at 15 minutes instead of running indefinitely. Behavior on normal-speed transfers is unchanged because `readIdleTimeoutMs` still fires first for slow-but-progressing body chunks.
- Slow transfers that genuinely exceed 15 minutes will now fail intentionally — this is the documented bounded-media contract.

## Evidence

### Live behavior proof (real HTTP server, real fetch, real AbortSignal, surfaced error shape)

Ran a standalone live script (`proof-103209-tool-run.mts`) via `tsx` that starts a real Node.js `http.createServer` (accepts the connection but never sends response headers) and calls `loadWebMediaRaw` against `http://127.0.0.1:<port>/photo.png` using the **default `fetch`** (no `fetchImpl` override) with `timeoutMs = 500ms` and `readIdleTimeoutMs = 30_000ms` — the same forwarding shape the image/pdf/image-generate tools use. The production code path uses `15 * 60_000`; the demo uses 500ms so the script completes quickly, but the code path (`loadWebMediaRaw` → `readRemoteMediaBuffer` → `fetchGuardedMediaResponse` → `fetchWithSsrFGuard` → `buildTimeoutAbortSignal` → `init.signal` → `globalThis.fetch`) is identical.

Local fallback run (Crabbox unavailable in this env):

```
$ tsx ./proof-103209-tool-run.mts
[proof] stalled HTTP server listening on http://127.0.0.1:45283
[proof] calling loadWebMediaRaw with timeoutMs=500ms (production code path uses 15*60_000)
[proof] this is the same path the image/pdf/image-generate tools exercise:
[proof]   image-tool.ts -> loadWebMedia -> loadWebMediaRaw -> readRemoteMediaBuffer
[proof]   -> fetchGuardedMediaResponse -> fetchWithSsrFGuard -> buildTimeoutAbortSignal
[fetch-timeout] fetch timeout after 500ms (elapsed 502ms) operation=fetchWithSsrFGuard url=http://127.0.0.1:45283/photo.png
[proof] elapsed: 598ms
[proof] surfaced error type: MediaFetchError
[proof] surfaced error.name: MediaFetchError
[proof] surfaced error.code: fetch_failed
[proof] surfaced error.message: Failed to fetch media from http://127.0.0.1:45283/photo.png: request timed out
[proof] surfaced error.cause.name: TimeoutError
[proof] surfaced error.cause.message: request timed out
[proof] result: timeout fired through real production path
[proof] this is the same error the image/pdf/image-generate tools surface to callers
```

Key observations:
- **502ms elapsed** (vs 500ms timeoutMs): the `[fetch-timeout]` log fires at the deadline, proving the AbortSignal fires at the configured timeout.
- **Surfaced error shape**: `MediaFetchError` with `code: "fetch_failed"` and `cause: TimeoutError("request timed out")` — this is the exact error the image/pdf/image-generate tool `execute` functions will throw when the underlying fetch stalls. The agent runtime will surface a clean "request timed out" error to the caller instead of hanging.

### Repository test (aborts a real stalled HTTP server via the overall timeoutMs deadline)

Added in `src/media/web-media.test.ts > aborts a real stalled HTTP server via the overall timeoutMs deadline`. The test starts a real Node.js HTTP server, withholds response headers, calls `loadWebMediaRaw`, and asserts:

1. The promise rejects (timeout fires).
2. Elapsed wall time is ≥ `timeoutMs - 50ms` and < `timeoutMs + 5s`.
3. The surfaced error has the exact shape: `MediaFetchError` with `code: "fetch_failed"`, message matching `/request timed out/i`, and `cause: TimeoutError`.

Focused suite run (local fallback — Crabbox unavailable in this env):

```
$ node scripts/run-vitest.mjs run src/media/web-media.test.ts --reporter=verbose
…
 ✓ |media| src/media/web-media.test.ts > loadWebMedia > aborts a real stalled HTTP server via the overall timeoutMs deadline 425ms
…

 Test Files  1 passed (1)
      Tests  76 passed (76)
```

### Canonical precedent

Merged #103266 (`src/cli/nodes-camera.ts:20`) established `15 * 60_000` as the bounded-media total-request lifetime for the "server never responds" stall class. This PR aligns the three agent-tool callers to the same ceiling.

### Tool-forwarding coverage

The three agent-tool test files now assert `timeoutMs: 15 * 60_000` forwarding alongside the existing `readIdleTimeoutMs` assertions:

- `src/agents/tools/image-tool.test.ts:2259`
- `src/agents/tools/image-generate-tool.test.ts`
- `src/agents/tools/pdf-tool.test.ts`

### Coordination with #103206

Both #103206 and this PR add the shared `WebMediaOptions.timeoutMs` seam because cross-repo fork PRs cannot stack on each other's fork branches — each must typecheck standalone. The intent is for #103206 to land first (it owns the seam + Tlon), then this PR reduces to the three agent-tool callers. The seam itself is identical (optional `timeoutMs?: number` after `readIdleTimeoutMs`, forwarded through `readRemoteMediaBuffer`).

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where users with heartbeat agents would receive leaked `HEARTBEAT_OK` text in their DM (routed agent) or hit `@heartbeat` / `chat not found` errors (isolated agent) when a heartbeat turn called the general `message` tool without an explicit recipient.

## Why This Change Was Made

Heartbeat turns inject ambient `From`/`To` context (a real delivery target or the non-deliverable `"heartbeat"` sentinel). Implicit message-tool target inference treated that ambient route as a recipient. The fix carries an explicit heartbeat-origin invariant: heartbeat embedded/CLI runs set `requireExplicitMessageTarget`, so no-target sends fail closed while intentional explicit-target notifications still work. Defense in depth also rejects the `"heartbeat"` sentinel during message-action normalization.

## User Impact

- Heartbeat runs no longer leak free-text acks into the source DM via the general `message` tool.
- Isolated heartbeat agents no longer attempt delivery to the literal `@heartbeat` handle.

target.body:
### Bug type

Regression (worked before, now fails)

### Beta release blocker

No

### Summary

Long-lived embedded sessions lose prompt-cache continuity across ambient group `room_event` turns, queued/compaction reconstruction, and native `openai-chatgpt-responses` continuation.

The reproduction uses strict room events:

```json
{
  "messages": {
    "groupChat": {
      "visibleReplies": "automatic",
      "unmentionedInbound": "room_event"
    }
  }
}
```

Unmentioned messages correctly require `message_tool_only` delivery. The regression is that current-turn delivery and sender policy also changed cache-visible prompt/tool state inside the same session. Some paths additionally dropped stable state during queueing or compaction, and built-in authenticated Responses sessions could replay full context instead of using native continuation.

### Steps to reproduce

1. Start OpenClaw 2026.6.11 with the configuration above.
2. In one Discord group/channel session, trigger an initial addressed turn.
3. Send unmentioned messages in the same session so they arrive as `room_event` turns.
4. Exercise queued work or compaction in the same session.
5. Compare serialized provider requests, prompt/tool digests, and cached-token metrics.
6. On native GPT-5.5 or GPT-5.6, inspect whether the second `openai-chatgpt-responses` request uses `previous_response_id` plus only new-turn input.

### Expected behavior

- Effective room-event delivery remains strict `message_tool_only`.
- Model-visible tool definitions, ordering, descriptions, and schemas stay stable when sender/event access changes.
- A trusted full current-turn access-policy snapshot appears when permissions or model context change.
- Runtime authorization blocks unavailable protected tools before side effects.
- Queue, memory, compaction, reconstruction, and fallback restore complete policy state.
- Built-in authenticated Responses sessions use native continuation; custom streams retain their routing.

### Actual behavior

Sanitized original same-session traces showed:

| turn | kind | prompt tokens | cached tokens |
| --- | --- | ---: | ---: |
| 1 | session start | 46,540 | 0 |
| 2 | room_event | 46,826 | 9,856 |
| 3 | room_event | 47,590 | 2,048 |

target.title: fix(tts): defer text settlement for final-mode TTS to eliminate churn (#83511)
target.body:
## Summary

When `messages.tts.mode = "final"`, the Telegram bot exhibited text "churn" — users would briefly see a text message appear, then it would be deleted and replaced by a voice note with the same text as caption. This happened on **both** the ACP dispatch path and the non-ACP dispatch path (`dispatch-from-config.ts`).

This PR eliminates the churn on **both paths** by introducing a `captionedFinalText` channel capability, suppressing live block delivery and partial streaming when captioned final TTS will be used, and correctly handling tagged auto-TTS mode with a split eligibility boolean.

## Root cause

```
Before (main):
  1. Block text / partial streaming delivers text to user immediately
  2. TTS synthesis runs (2-5 seconds)
  3. Voice note + caption delivered as separate message
  Result: user sees text first, then voice note = churn (#83511)

After (this PR):
  1. willUseCaptionedFinalTts = true (channel supports captioned voice + final TTS mode)
  2. Partial streaming suppressed, block text delivery suppressed
  3. TTS synthesis runs, text accumulated silently
  4. Voice note + caption delivered as single message (or text fallback if TTS fails)
  Result: user sees only the voice note with caption = no churn
```

### Tagged auto-TTS mode

When `messages.tts.auto: "tagged"`, TTS only fires for replies containing `[[tts:...]]` directives. Three additional issues were discovered and fixed:

1. **Split boolean**: `willUseCaptionedFinalTts` was doing two jobs — gating live text suppression AND caption eligibility. Split into `willUseCaptionedFinalTts` (live text suppression, excludes tagged) and `canCaptionFinalTts` (caption eligibility, includes tagged).

2. **Block TTS gate**: The accumulated block TTS fallback was gated on `replies.length === 0`, but Anthropic streaming returns both block callbacks and a final reply payload. Changed to gate on `deliveredFinalTtsMedia` and `queuedFinal` instead.

3. **Partial streaming leak**: `onPartialReply` was active for tagged mode, sending raw `[[tts:text]]...[[/tts:text]]` directive text to Telegram during streaming, creating a duplicate text message before the voice+caption arrived. Fixed by gating `onPartialReply` with `canCaptionFinalTts` (covers both always and tagged modes) instead of `willUseCaptionedFinalTts`.

### Media block preservation

When captioned final TTS is active, block suppression is narrowed to **text-only** payloads. Blocks containing media (`mediaUrl`, `mediaUrls`), `presentation`, `interactive`, or `channelData` are delivered immediately with their text stripped (to avoid duplicating the caption). This applies to both ACP and non-ACP dispatch paths.

## Changes

| File | Change |
|------|--------|
| `src/auto-reply/reply/dispatch-from-config.ts` | `willUseCaptionedFinalTts` + `canCaptionFinalTts`: suppress partial streaming and block text for both always and tagged modes; narrow block suppression to text-only payloads (media blocks delivered with text stripped); `sendFinalPayload` returns `deliveredMedia`; block TTS gate changed from `replies.length === 0` to `!deliveredFinalTtsMedia && !queuedFinal` |
| `src/auto-reply/reply/dispatch-from-config.test.ts` | Regression tests: tagged directive-only voice+caption, tagged+always both-block-and-final delivery, partial suppression for tagged TTS on caption-capable channels, plain tagged block delivery, media block delivery with text stripped, text-only block suppression |
| `src/auto-reply/reply/dispatch-acp.ts` | `willUseCaptionedFinalTts` gate: suppress ACP block delivery and defer text settlement; `canCaptionFinalTts` for tagged mode; `deliveredFinalTtsMedia` tracking |
| `src/auto-reply/reply/dispatch-acp-delivery.ts` | `deliveredFinalTtsMedia` state tracking + `hasDeliveredFinalTtsMedia()` accessor; narrow `suppressBlockUserDelivery` to text-only blocks (media blocks delivered with text stripped) |
| `src/auto-reply/reply/dispatch-acp-delivery.test.ts` | Regression tests: media block delivery with text stripped under `suppressBlockUserDelivery`, text-only block suppression |
| `src/auto-reply/reply/dispatch-acp.test.ts` | Regression tests: deferred settlement, block suppression, tagged streaming, tagged directive TTS, ACP live text deferral |
| `src/auto-reply/reply/acp-projector.ts` | `deferLiveTextUntilFinalFlush` option to suppress live text flushing for tagged TTS |
| `src/tts/directives.ts` | `resolveDirectiveOnlyTtsCaptionText` parser helper to extract clean caption from directive-only responses |
| `extensions/telegram/src/shared.ts` | `captionedFinalText: true` capability declaration |
| `extensions/telegram/src/shared.test.ts` | Test for capability declaration |
| `src/channels/plugins/types.core.ts` | JSDoc for `captionedFinalText` capability contract |
| `src/channels/plugins/tts-capabilities.test.ts` | Capability seam test |
| `docs/tools/tts.md` | Document `captionedFinalText` capability: opt-in criteria via `capabilities.tts.voice`, tagged mode behavior, text-only fallback, plugin API snippet |
| `docs/plugins/sdk-channel-plugins.md` | Document `captionedFinalText` capability in channel plugin SDK guide: opt-in declaration, media block preservation, fallback behavior, tagged mode |
| `docs/.generated/plugin-sdk-api-baseline.sha256` | Updated SDK API baseline hash |

## Tests

```
$ npx vitest run src/auto-reply/reply/dispatch-from-config.test.ts
 ✓ 272 passed (272)

$ npx vitest run src/auto-reply/reply/dispatch-acp-delivery.test.ts
 ✓ 38 passed (38)

$ npx vitest run src/auto-reply/reply/dispatch-acp.test.ts
 ✓ 67 passed (67)

$ npx vitest run src/auto-reply/reply/dispatch-from-config.reply-dispatch.test.ts src/auto-reply/reply/dispatch-from-config.final-outcome-counts.test.ts src/auto-reply/reply/dispatch-from-config.acp-abort.test.ts
 ✓ 26 passed (26)   # settle-lifecycle paths, no hang

$ npx vitest run extensions/telegram/src/shared.test.ts
 ✓ 11 passed (11)

$ npx vitest run src/channels/plugins/tts-capabilities.test.ts
 ✓ 1 passed (1)
```

## Real behavior proof

- **Behavior or issue addressed**: Telegram TTS final-mode text-before-voice churn on both ACP and non-ACP dispatch paths, plus tagged mode partial preview leaking raw `[[tts:text]]` directives, plus media block suppression during captioned final TTS.

- **Real environment tested**: Local patched OpenClaw checkout at commit `05b4483a8f`, macOS arm64, Node.js v24.10.0. Live Telegram bot (`@thomas_fu_bot`) with Microsoft TTS (`zh-CN-XiaoxiaoNeural`), `messages.tts.mode: "final"`.

- **Failing proof before fix (live Telegram)**:

  ![Before fix — separate text message + voice message (churn)](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Jerry-Xin/openclaw/proof-images-83988/.proof-images/83988-before-fix.png)

  User sent "hello" to the Telegram bot. The bot responded with **two separate messages**: a text message AND a voice note — instead of a single voice note with caption.

- **Exact steps or command run after this patch**:
  1. Built and installed from current head: `npm run build && npm pack && npm install -g openclaw-2026.6.2.tgz`
  2. Registered and restarted Gateway: `openclaw gateway install && openclaw gateway restart`
  3. Tested with `messages.tts.auto: "always"` and `messages.tts.auto: "tagged"` — sent plain messages and directive-bearing messages to `@thomas_fu_bot` on Telegram

- **Evidence after fix**: Always mode (`messages.tts.auto: "always"`) at commit `05b4483a8f`:

  ![Always mode — voice with caption, single message](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Jerry-Xin/openclaw/proof-images-83988/.proof-images/83988-always-mode.png)

  Always-mode replies produce a single voice note with caption text. No text churn, no separate text bubble.

- **Evidence — Media block preservation with captioned final TTS at commit `05b4483a8f`**:

  ![Media block preserved — image delivered + voice note with caption](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Jerry-Xin/openclaw/proof-images-83988/.proof-images/83988-media-block.png)

  When the bot generates an image during a TTS-enabled conversation (`auto: "always"`), the image is delivered immediately while text is deferred to the voice note caption. No media blocks are suppressed, and caption text does not duplicate as a separate text message.

- **Observed result after fix**: Always TTS auto mode delivers voice notes as single messages with caption text on Telegram. Media blocks (images, files) are preserved and delivered immediately with text stripped. No text flash, no duplicate messages, no media loss.

- **What was not tested**: Other TTS providers (only Microsoft TTS tested live). Group chat TTS (tested in DM only). Other channels with `captionedFinalText` capability (only Telegram tested). Tagged mode live proof pending — covered by unit tests (partial suppression + directive-only caption regression tests added).

## Settle-lifecycle reconciliation (rebased onto current main)

Current `main` made the delivered-transcript mirror fire-and-forget so reply completion no longer blocks on `dispatcher.waitForIdle()`. An earlier revision of this PR gated the captioned-final text fallback on an inline `await dispatcher.waitForIdle()` inside the reply operation, which would reintroduce exactly that completion-vs-idle block.

The fallback now rides the same dispatcher settle lifecycle instead of an inline wait:

- The direct-dispatcher and synthesized-voice paths keep their optimistic queued gating and capture the pre-send final-outcome counts.
- When a captioned final (or its synthesized-voice sibling) is admitted through the raw dispatcher, a post-settlement task is registered via `registerReplyDispatcherSettledTask` — the same seam the transcript mirror uses. It runs after `waitForIdle()` inside `settleReplyDispatcher`, out of the reply hot path.
- That task compares the post-settlement final-outcome counts against the pre-send snapshot; if the captioned voice failed or cancelled asynchronously it re-sends the accumulated block text as a text-only final, so suppressed content is never silently dropped. On success it does nothing, so there is no duplicate text.

This preserves the churn fix and the async-failure text fallback while keeping reply completion off `waitForIdle`, so the fire-and-forget contract from the current transcript-mirror behavior is not regressed.

### Cancelled final delivery (not just failed)

A `beforeDeliver` / `reply_payload_sending` hook returning `null` **cancels** a send after `enqueue()` has already reported acceptance. That outcome is tracked as *cancelled*, not *failed* (`getCancelledCounts()` vs `getFailedCounts()` on the dispatcher). The ACP direct-visible-text settlement previously folded only failed counts into its undelivered accounting, so a cancelled captioned voice final left `finalMediaDelivered` set and skipped the deferred text fallback — silently dropping the reply text (the block text was already suppressed for the captioned path).

The settlement now folds cancelled block/final counts alongside failed counts (`settleDirectVisibleText` in `dispatch-acp-delivery.ts`, via a new `readDispatcherCancelledCounts` reader mirroring the failed reader). A cancelled captioned voice final therefore clears `finalMediaDelivered` and the deferred text fallback delivers the accumulated text. The non-ACP settle-lifecycle path already folded cancelled outcomes and is unchanged. A regression test drives an asynchronously cancelled captioned voice on Telegram and asserts the plain-text fallback fires.

Closes #83511

target.title: fix(gateway): reconcile on-disk config after watcher recreate (#103729)
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

The gateway watches `openclaw.json` for hot-reload. When that watcher hits an error (for example EMFILE/ENOSPC inotify exhaustion) it is closed and re-created after a backoff. The re-created watcher is built with `ignoreInitial: true` and no reconciliation read, so any config edit made by an **external process** while no watcher is alive (the error-recovery down window) — a manual edit, or a separate `openclaw doctor --fix` run, neither of which routes through the running gateway's in-process write channel — is silently adopted as the new watcher's baseline and **never scheduled for reload**. The gateway keeps running the stale pre-edit config indefinitely, with no log distinguishing a missed change from a normal quiet period. This is exactly the population the inotify-exhaustion retries exist to serve.

Closes #103729

## Why This Change Was Made

`ignoreInitial: true` is correct for the very first watcher (startup already reads and applies the config). On **recreation**, however, there is an interval with no live watcher during which an on-disk change can occur, and the new watcher's `ignoreInitial: true` guarantees that change produces no event. Both recreate paths share the defect: the native-retry timer and the polling-degrade timer.

## Changes

- `createWatcher` gains an optional `reconcile` parameter. When `true`, it reconciles **once the recreated watcher emits `ready`** — i.e. after chokidar has finished its asynchronous initial scan and established its baseline — by scheduling one read (`scheduleAfter(0)`) of the current on-disk config through the existing scheduler (the canonical seam that owns snapshot reads, validation, diffing, and application). Reconciling on `ready` (rather than eagerly, right after `chokidar.watch()` returns) guarantees any edit that landed during the down window or the initial scan is on disk before the read, closing the construction→`ready` window. A `watcher !== next` guard drops the callback if the watcher was already replaced or stopped.
- Both recreate timers (native-retry and polling-degrade) now call `createWatcher(true)`. The initial startup `createWatcher()` is unchanged, since startup already read and applied the config before the first watcher existed.
- The watcher test mock now models `once` and the `ready` event; two regression tests cover both recreate paths and assert the reconcile fires only after `ready`.

## User Impact

External config edits (manual, or `openclaw doctor --fix`) that land while the watcher is recovering from an inotify/EMFILE error are now applied after the watcher is re-created, instead of being silently dropped until some later unrelated write touches the file again.

## Evidence

**Real behavior proof.** Drove the real `startGatewayConfigReloader` against a real on-disk `openclaw.json` with a real chokidar watcher. A real `error` event was emitted on the live watcher (as inotify exhaustion would raise it); the watcher, the file, the debounce/reload loop, and `readSnapshot` reading the file all stayed real. An external edit (`{"v":3}`) was written during the backoff gap while **no watcher was alive**. Chokidar was run in polling mode, whose down-window semantics are deterministic and cross-platform (a polling watcher snapshots the file at start and `ignoreInitial` suppresses that baseline; an edit predating the watch is folded into the baseline and never emits) — the same silent drop the issue author observed under native Linux inotify, which likewise does not replay events that predate the watch. Timeline (`[ms] event`):

```
# BEFORE (true origin/main, no reconcile)
[0187] watch#0 constructed
[0199] watch#0 EVENT ready
[1113] watch#1 constructed        # recreate after backoff
[1114] watch#1 EVENT ready
reads_after_recreate=0
downwindow_edit(v3)_ever_read=false
raw_config_contents_read=[]        # v3 silently dropped

# AFTER (this PR, identical inputs)
[0015] watch#0 constructed
[0023] watch#0 EVENT ready
[0941] watch#1 constructed        # recreate after backoff
[0941] watch#1 EVENT ready
[0965] readSnapshot -> {"v":3}     # reconcile fires AFTER ready
reads_after_recreate=1
downwindow_edit(v3)_ever_read=true
raw_config_contents_read=["{\"v\":3}"]
```

The reconcile read (965ms) occurs strictly after the recreated watcher's `ready` (941ms), demonstrating the readiness gating.

**Focused tests.** Two tests in `config-reload.test.ts` assert a reconcile read runs after both recreate paths (native retry + polling degrade), and only after the recreated watcher's `ready` event (nothing is read before `ready`). Full suite green:

```
$ npx vitest run src/gateway/config-reload.test.ts
 Test Files  3 passed (3)
      Tests  267 passed (267)
```

target.title: gateway: failed plugin reload leaves current plugin metadata describing a plugin set that never loaded
target.body:
## Summary

During a gateway plugin hot reload, the process-global "current plugin metadata" handoff is committed to the next/attempted plugin set before the fallible plugin rebuild runs, and there is no rollback if the rebuild fails. When the rebuild throws (the error is swallowed by the reload catch), the live plugin runtime keeps executing the old, still-loaded plugin code, but every caller that consults the current plugin metadata now answers questions about plugin availability, declared capabilities, and contracts using the new plugin manifest that never actually loaded. The divergence persists for the life of the process.

## Environment

- Commit: 9b4c7c0991dddb77295453259b433122e705bfb4 (origin/main at time of filing)
- Surface: Gateway plugin hot reload (`reloadAttachedGatewayPlugins`), and every consumer of the process-global current plugin metadata (manifest-driven tool/provider capability availability, model-catalog, provider-auth-alias, plugin-skills).

## Steps to reproduce

1. Gateway is running with plugin X v1; its manifest contracts declare capability set A (for example an image-generation provider).
2. Operator upgrades X to v2 declaring a different capability set (for example dropping image-generation and adding video-generation), or re-installs the same id with a registration that will fail to load. The config write triggers `plan.reloadPlugins`.
3. `reloadAttachedGatewayPlugins` builds `nextPluginLookUpTable` from v2 and calls `setCurrentPluginMetadataSnapshot(nextPluginLookUpTable, ...)` at `src/gateway/server.impl.ts:1437`, switching the process-global current metadata to describe v2's capabilities.
4. `prepareGatewayPluginLoad(...)` at `src/gateway/server.impl.ts:1442` (the fallible module load/registration step) throws. The exception propagates up and is swallowed by `runReload`'s catch at `src/gateway/config-reload.ts:395` (logged only).
5. `replaceAttachedPluginRuntime(loaded)` at `src/gateway/server.impl.ts:1458` never runs, so the gateway keeps executing plugin X v1's real code and tools. But every subsequent `resolvePluginMetadataSnapshot` / `getCurrentPluginMetadataSnapshot` caller now answers using v2's manifest-declared capabilities, which do not match what is running, with no error surfaced.

## Expected

If the plugin rebuild fails and the runtime stays on the previously loaded plugin code, the process-global current plugin metadata must also stay describing the previously loaded plugin set. A failed reload should be a no-op for both the runtime registry and the metadata handoff.

## Actual

The metadata handoff is committed to the attempted plugin set at `server.impl.ts:1437`, before the fallible rebuild at `:1442`. On failure it is never rolled back, so the metadata permanently describes a plugin version/capability set that never loaded while the runtime executes the old one. Capability-availability decisions can then silently offer a tool the running code does not support, or silently withhold one it does support.

## Root cause (if known)

`reloadAttachedGatewayPlugins` in `src/gateway/server.impl.ts` orders the reload so the process-global metadata handoff is committed before the fallible rebuild, with no rollback:

```ts
// src/gateway/server.impl.ts
const nextPluginLookUpTable = loadPluginLookUpTable({ ... });   // 1397
// ...
setCurrentPluginMetadataSnapshot(nextPluginLookUpTable, {       // 1437  committed FIRST
  config: params.nextConfig,
  env: process.env,
  workspaceDir: defaultWorkspaceDir,
});
const loaded = prepareGatewayPluginLoad({ ... });              // 1442  fallible rebuild AFTER
// ...
replaceAttachedPluginRuntime(loaded);                          // 1458  runtime swap AFTER
```

`setCurrentPluginMetadataSnapshot` writes the single-slot Gateway-owned handoff documented at `src/plugins/current-plugin-metadata-snapshot.ts:44-45` ("Single-slot Gateway-owned handoff... never accumulate historical metadata snapshots here"). That slot is what answers "what plugins/capabilities/contracts currently exist" for callers via `resolvePluginMetadataSnapshot`'s fast path (`getCurrentPluginMetadataSnapshot`, `src/plugins/plugin-metadata-snapshot.ts:638-673`), including tool/provider availability in `src/agents/tools/manifest-capability-availability.ts` (image/video/music generation and media understanding).

A capture/restore pair for exactly this slot already exists (`captureCurrentPluginMetadataSnapshotState` / `restoreCurrentPluginMetadataSnapshotState`, `src/plugins/current-plugin-metadata-snapshot.ts:126-160`), but it is used nowhere in the reload path. `server.impl.ts:49` imports only `setCurrentPluginMetadataSnapshot`. The pair's only non-test caller in the whole repo is an unrelated CLI command that temporarily overrides the slot for a scoped query (`src/commands/models/list.status-command.ts:185` and `:192`). The ready-made fix is to capture the current state before `setCurrentPluginMetadataSnapshot` at `:1437` and restore it if `prepareGatewayPluginLoad` (or the subsequent runtime swap) throws, so a failed reload leaves the metadata handoff on the still-running plugin set.

## Sibling surfaces

Findings for this reload path share one root incident (reload ordering with no rollback) across two separate files:

- This issue: the metadata handoff no-rollback in `src/gateway/server.impl.ts` (`reloadAttachedGatewayPlugins`).
- A sibling PR is being opened for the loader-side no-rollback in `src/plugins/loader.ts` (`loadOpenClawPlugins`), where the fallible module load itself leaves partial state behind.

These are two distinct bugs in two distinct files and should be tracked separately. This issue is distinct from PR #89824 (closed), which guarded `src/gateway/config-reload-plan.ts` against a malformed plugin registration getter throwing during reload rule planning, a different file and mechanism. It is also distinct from issue #103736 (open), which is about `getRuntimeConfig` being flipped ahead of hooks/cron during a deferred channel restart, not the plugin metadata handoff.

## Real behavior proof

Behavior addressed: On a failed plugin reload the process-global current plugin metadata is left describing the attempted plugin set that never loaded, while the runtime keeps running the old plugin code.
Real environment tested: Drove the real production metadata handoff functions (`setCurrentPluginMetadataSnapshot`, `getCurrentPluginMetadataSnapshot`, `captureCurrentPluginMetadataSnapshotState`, `restoreCurrentPluginMetadataSnapshotState`) from `src/plugins/current-plugin-metadata-snapshot.ts` at commit 9b4c7c0991dddb77295453259b433122e705bfb4, replicating the exact `reloadAttachedGatewayPlugins` ordering (commit-then-fallible-rebuild) with the rebuild throwing, matching the swallowed error path.
Exact steps or command run after this patch: Drive the real handoff functions in the two orderings: (BEFORE) commit next metadata, then run the fallible rebuild which throws and is swallowed, no rollback; (AFTER) capture current state, commit next metadata, run the fallible rebuild which throws, restore on failure. After each, read back the running metadata's declared plugin version and capability contracts.
Evidence after fix:
```
# OBSERVED (buggy, current main ordering)
startup, v1 running:            running-metadata=acme-media@1.0.0 contracts=[imageGenerationProviders]
reload failed, error swallowed: v2 module discovery/registration failed
runtime registry swapped to v2? false (v1 code still executing)
after failed reload:            running-metadata=acme-media@2.0.0 contracts=[videoGenerationProviders]

# EXPECTED (fix: capture before commit, restore on failure)
startup, v1 running:            running-metadata=acme-media@1.0.0 contracts=[imageGenerationProviders]
reload failed, error swallowed: v2 module discovery/registration failed
runtime registry swapped to v2? false (v1 code still executing)
after failed reload:            running-metadata=acme-media@1.0.0 contracts=[imageGenerationProviders]
```
Observed result after fix: On current main, after a swallowed reload failure the runtime registry is never swapped (v1 code still executing) yet the process-global current plugin metadata answers acme-media@2.0.0 with videoGenerationProviders, a capability set that never loaded and does not match the running v1 code; with the existing capture/restore pair applied the metadata rolls back to acme-media@1.0.0 with imageGenerationProviders, matching the running code.
What was not tested: The full gateway process was not stood up end to end; the repro drives the real metadata handoff functions and replicates the `reloadAttachedGatewayPlugins` ordering with a throwing rebuild rather than instantiating the whole gateway. The downstream user-visible effect (a specific media-generation tool being offered or withheld) was not exercised through a live agent turn.

## Summary

This PR tightens the existing compatible-bundle MCP path for bundles that need a narrower default tool surface.

- Adds regression coverage that a Codex-compatible bundle `.mcp.json` preserves `toolFilter.include`, `toolFilter.exclude`, and a relative bundle data root.
- Documents bundle MCP tool filters on the plugin-bundles page alongside the existing transport and tool-naming guidance.
- Keeps scope limited to bundle MCP loading/docs; runtime filtering behavior already exists and is covered separately.

Reviewers should focus on whether the bundle MCP docs accurately describe the existing runtime behavior and whether the new compatible-bundle regression is useful.

## Linked context

No issue filed.

Related precedent investigated: bundle MCP support and follow-up coverage in prior OpenClaw PRs such as #48611, #71287, #79686, and #88399. This PR follows that existing bundle MCP seam.

## Real behavior proof (required for external PRs)

Behavior addressed: Compatible bundles that contribute MCP servers can ship a narrow default tool surface through `toolFilter.include` and `toolFilter.exclude`; OpenClaw docs now describe that bundle path and a regression test proves the loader preserves the filter and relative app root.

- This PR updates the remaining stale references to `memory/**/*.md`. No runtime behavior change.

## Files touched
- `extensions/memory-core/index.ts` — lazy `memory_search` / `memory_get` descriptors
- `extensions/memory-core/src/tools.ts` — concrete `memory_search` / `memory_get` descriptions
